prompt: In a café survey, $P(\text{orders coffee}) = 0.4$, $P(\text{orders a pastry}) = 0.5$, and $P(\text{orders both}) = 0.2$. Are ordering coffee and ordering a pastry independent events?

choices.label: No, because a customer can order both
No, because $0.4 + 0.5 - 0.2$ is not equal to $1$
Yes, because the two probabilities are different

hint: Independence is a calculation, not a feeling. Test: does $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$?

hints.text: Independence is a calculation, not a feeling. Test: does $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$?
$0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2 = P(\text{both})$, so the events are independent: choice A.

explanation: Two events are independent when $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$.
So coffee and pastry orders are independent. Choice A. (Being able to order both is about overlap, not independence, so B is wrong.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Check with conditional probability
steps: That equals $P(\text{pastry}) = 0.5$: knowing someone ordered coffee does not change the pastry chance.
Unchanged conditional probability is exactly what independence means.
